content.text:
Plan a story of about 3500 words from this premise.

Write a tragic love story about a lord's daughter falling in love with a servant, 3500 words.

Propose about 4 scenes of roughly 875 words each. Give every character, location and significant object a stable id now — later scenes can only refer to entities that exist. State the world rules the story must not break. Then call submit_plan.

entities.sketch: Elys Harrow: the lord's only daughter, nineteen. Curious and quietly fierce, raised inside Harrowhold; she knows the rules but has never loved any of them.
Garr: a stable-hand/servant in his early twenties. Steady, taciturn, surprisingly gentle and practical; he knows the estate's edges and a few books stolen nights in the clerk's light.
Lord Harrow: Elys's father, late forties, widower and master of Harrowhold. Stern, status-minded, believes household order is the only safe thing for his line.
Marta: Elys's maid and confidante, thirty, pragmatic and loyal. Knows the household's gossip and the thin places where rules fray; she becomes a reluctant accomplice.
Aldric of Westbrook: the suitor Lord Harrow selects, mid-twenties, polished and useful to the alliance Harrow wants. Not cruel but not Elys's match; his presence forces the lovers' choices.
Rowan: captain of the household guard, early thirties. Professional, feels the tension between duty and conscience; carries orders without asking too many questions — at least at first.
Harrowhold: the lord's manor — stone house with a great hall, a high balcony over the gardens, a walled garden, stables and a paved courtyard. It is both a home and a small, ordered world.
The walled garden of Harrowhold: a secluded patch of fruit trees, clipped hedges and an old stone bench. The garden is where unequal people can meet unseen if they dare.
The west balcony of Elys's chamber: overlooking the gardens, a narrow, sheltered ledge where conversations can be lowered into the night.
The great hall: the center of household life, where proclamations are made, alliances announced and the social choreography of the estate is performed.
The paved courtyard before the servants' door and stables. A gateway between worlds and, in this story's end, the place where order will be publicly enforced.
An ivory hairpin, carved with a tiny willow motif. Elys's keepsake; it becomes the lovers' token and the object that fuses intimacy to consequence.
A folded and sealed note: an earnest, simple message from Garr that will be intercepted. The letter is a practical attempt at arranging escape that becomes evidence.

arguments.logline: In the austere halls of Harrowhold, Lord Harrow's daughter Elys falls for Garr, a stable-hand; their tender, clandestine love collides with duty and status when a marriage is arranged for Elys. A betrayed plan and an intercepted letter force a cruel choice: order will be upheld at the expense of the two who loved across the divide.

scenes.intent: Introduce the household, social order and the first meeting that sets the tragedy in motion. Show Elys's confinement and Garr's small freedoms; have Elys drop or lend her ivory hairpin to Garr (obj-hairpin-ivory) as a private token. Establish Marta as a watcher/confidante and Lord Harrow's distant, controlling presence. End on the lovers' quiet promise — not legally binding, but intimate and absolute to them.

Deepen the relationship through secret meetings on the balcony and in the garden. Let them share stories that reveal their incompatibility with the world around them (her expected marriage, his limited future). Use Marta to assist or cover for them, and let the hairpin be both comfort and proof of affection. Introduce Aldric's name as the man Lord Harrow has in mind without yet staging the betrothal. End with Garr drafting (or promising to draft) a note proposing escape — the letter (obj-letter-sealed) is prepared but not yet delivered.

Raise the stakes: Lord Harrow announces Elys's betrothal to Aldric in the great hall. Publicly the household swells with congratulation and obligation; privately Elys and Garr plan a desperate elopement. The letter (obj-letter-sealed) is intercepted — either by Marta under coercion or by the guard — and shown to Lord Harrow. Captain Rowan is given an order to apprehend Garr. Show the moral conflict in Rowan and Marta's torment at betraying the lovers. End with Garr being taken from the stables/courtyard to face Lord Harrow's judgement.

Deliver the tragic payoff. In the courtyard, Garr is punished according to the household law Lord Harrow enforces; the punishment must be final and public (execution or banishment is the choice the prose will make). Elys, in a last desperate act, attempts to intervene or join him — using the hairpin (obj-hairpin-ivory) as a physical link to what was theirs — and the scene ends in irreversible loss. Explore the aftermath: Lord Harrow's hollow victory; Marta and Rowan's guilt; the burnt-out shape of Elys's choice. The scene must feel inevitable in retrospect: each earlier choice pushed it toward this end.

world_rules: No supernatural elements or anachronistic technology — the story is grounded in a quasi-medieval household world.

Household law: the lord has the social and legal authority within his household to arrange his heir's marriage and to punish servants for crimes (including conspiracy or aiding escape). Secret tokens or promises carry emotional meaning only; they confer no legal standing.

Marriage is a legal/sacral act that requires the lord's approval (or a priest with jurisdiction). A clandestine private promise between a noble and a servant does not create a recognized marriage in this world.

Social mobility is limited: servants cannot inherit land or titles; they can be freed, bound, or punished, but any change to status must be explicitly recorded if it is to be a fact later in the manuscript.
No deus ex machina: once a scene sets a fact (a letter intercepted, an order given), later scenes must carry its consequences — events are causal and traceable.
Objects introduced (hairpin, sealed letter) are physical evidence: their existence, who possesses them, and any inscriptions or marks must be recorded in the index if later referenced.

Elys steps onto the balcony like a person returning to a habit—careful, as if the wood itself could take offence. The west wind smells of cut herbs and the distant smoke of the kitchens; below, Garr waits by the clipped yew where the hedge makes a dark pocket. Marta is already at the far end of the walk, a shadow among shadows, smiling at no one as she hooks a tray to the wrong hand and sends the corridor maid the other way.

"Your hands are cold," Garr says when she leans on the rail. He fingers at the edge of his palm where the ivory rests; the little willow catches a slant of light and goes all green in the sheen.

She laughs, the sound small against the night. "They mean to call him Aldric, step one of everything," she says, and the name is a stone dropped into their conversation. "They say Lord Harrow is pleased. He said at table—'Aldric brings Westbrook's levies and a fine marriage with no scandal.'"

Garr's mouth tightens where it always tightens when the house says its plans out loud. "Westbrook's levies won't carry my name anywhere but a ledger," he says, and there is no bitterness in it, only the plainness of his life pulled into view: tack mended, oats counted, no title to offer.

Marta stands a pace away, hands busy with a folded napkin, and yet her attention is the sort that keeps a clock. She keeps the watch that is not writing down names. When a serving girl passes, Marta trips her with a smile and a question; the sweep is delayed, the corridor quieted. She looks at Elys and the resigned line on her mouth becomes a promise of small crimes.

Elys presses her palm against the rail until the wood cools her fingers. Garr lifts his hand to meet hers and closes it over the willow pin as if she had lent him a piece of her life. He does not put the pin away; he keeps it in his palm like a vow.

"Take it, Garr," she says—the same three words that have already learned the weight of saying—and he lets his hand close on them tighter. The pin is smooth and faintly warm.

Conversation moves past names into the small geography of what they might dare. "What would you do if we ran?" she asks, looking down where the stable-roof splashes black against the fields.

Garr huffs a breath that is almost a laugh. "I know the back lanes, the river and the mill. I can take a horse and find a plough to hide behind. But I will not be a lord's son in any ledger, and I know enough to keep a roof over a head. That is the edge I stand on. I am not the sort to promise more than bread." He shrugs; the admission is not defeat but a map.

Marta lets out a sound—half-scoff, half-care—before she leans forward and lays out practical things as if she were listing stitches. "You have a narrow hour after vespers when the house is noisy and a good fence in the east hedge where the ground dips. I can leave the west shutters unlatched and tell Jory that the pantry is missing a tray. I will not be an accomplice in a sermon, but I will put you outside the notice of men who count names." She speaks quickly, the way someone who has weighed risk and found it possible will speak.

Elys snatches at the plan the way a child snatches at a borrowed coin. "If your father hears—" She cannot finish; the balcony's night swallows the words where the rest of the household sleeps under Lord Harrow's quiet hand.

"He will say that Aldric is sensible and useful," Marta says, softer now. "He does not count hearts. He counts advantage."

Garr watches Elys as she traces the willow's carved leaves with a fingertip. "Then if we go," he says, putting a steadiness into the word, "we go on what I can promise. I'll write. I'll fold a note and seal it honest with wax. If I put it where only I can find it, you'll know I mean it."

He takes from his pouch a small scrap of folded paper—neat, practical as his life—and with a coin he presses the wax to the corner. The wax is plain and warm and the fold closes like something decided. He tucks the sealed scrap beneath the leather of his tunic and lays his fingers flat over it, as one might over a small, living thing.

"I'll write it tonight," he says to Elys, and the sentence feels like a ladder rung offered to a hand.

Elys nods, eyes bright as though she has built a house from the light of his promise. Marta watches them both, the lines around her mouth speaking of what she will bear. When they part, it is by rehearsed motions: Garr slipping down the path toward the stables with the willow-pin a secret in his hand, Elys drawing back to the balcony and the rooms that smell of lavender and rule. The east hedge holds its dark; the house keeps its long, slow order. In the pocket where the wax sits, the letter waits like a small, patient thing.

dropped. A scene-level gate cannot see any of them, because each individual scene
is fine.

The plan is written to .orchestrator/revision-plan.md. Read it, then read what it
points at — you have the whole book under novel/chapters/ and the promise ledger
at continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl.

Two constraints, and they are what make this hard rather than tedious. Every scene
after a defect is already written and was written against it, so a repair that
contradicts a later scene trades a known defect for an unknown one. And a payoff
dropped in at the deadline with no preparation reads worse than the abandonment it
was meant to repair.

So do not rewrite anything now. Say, for each task: whether it is real, what the
fix would have to touch, and whether the fix is worth its risk. Record anything
you would do differently next time with `remember` — the next story is where that
judgement is worth something.

arguments.body: Lesson: When a scene establishes an intimate or plot-bearing promise (private vows, escape plans, sealed notes), record alongside it an explicit expected payoff (scene id or chapter) or else mark the promise as intentionally ambiguous/breakable. Rationale: the whole-story pass commonly finds ‘intimate promises’ left unpaid; either payoffs must be planned across the span or the text must foreshadow their failure so the absence reads as design, not neglect. Procedure to adopt next time: 1) Whenever a scene creates a promise added to continuity/plot-contracts, include an 'expected_payoff' field (scene id or 'deferred') and an 'alternative_outcome' flag (true/false). 2) If alternative_outcome=true, add at least one foreshadowing beat within two subsequent scenes. 3) Verify these fields in the planner’s pre-commit checklist so a promise does not land on the ledger without a traceable disposition. Based on s-001..s-004: the book intended a tragic denial, but the index lacks an explicit 'failed by design' record, which makes the unpaid promises appear as omissions rather than thematic choices.

I read the revision plan and the committed scenes. Below I treat each unpaid promise in turn: say whether it is a real defect, what a fix would have to touch (which files/scenes and what lines or beats), and whether the fix is worth its risk.

Summary judgement up front
- Both unpaid promises listed are real absences in the ledger: the manuscript as committed leaves the reader with no explicit, tracked payoff for either private vow. Both can be fixed with small, targeted clarifications; both fixes are low-risk to continuity if done as minimal, expository beats in s-004 (the final scene). I recommend fixing both — not because the story cannot be read as tragic omission, but because the index and the whole-story pass require explicit payoffs or an explicit record that the absence is deliberate.

Task 1 — “I will come back” / “I will wait” (from s-001)
- Is it real?
  - Yes. The promise is introduced verbatim in s-001 and never explicitly addressed as fulfilled or failed in the committed prose. The current ending (both lovers dead) implies the vow failed, but the ledger records the promise as unpaid because no scene explicitly registers that outcome.
- What a fix would have to touch
  - Where: novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-004.md (the final courtyard scene) is the best and safest place to reconcile this promise because it is the scene that already determines the lovers' fates.
  - What to add: one short, explicit beat near the end that references the original vow in language that ties it to the line recorded in the index. For example, a single sentence of reflection from Elys or a small exchange that uses the original phrasing (or a close echo): "You promised you'd come back," she had said long ago; now she knows he will not. Or, if she dies in the act, a line from Garr's last words that explicitly addresses the promise ("I came back—" or "I tried to come back—") would also close the loop.
  - Why this is minimal: it does not change any factual chain (the execution, the letter interception, the custody of objects) — it only records the emotional and causal relationship and makes the intended tragic failure explicit.
- Is the fix worth its risk?
  - Yes. Low risk and high payoff. It clarifies authorial intent and converts what reads as an omission into a deliberate tragic resolution. It also gives the continuity ledger an explicit provenance for the promise's outcome (s-004).

Task 2 — Garr's note promise: "I'll write it tonight" and the sealed letter (from s-002)
- Is it real?
  - Sort of. Garr literally writes and seals a note (the obj-letter-sealed) in s-002 and the letter is intercepted in s-003 and shown to Lord Harrow, which is recorded. The ledger flags this as an unpaid promise because the implied purpose of the letter—arranging escape/elopement—was not achieved for the lovers. As with Task 1, the manuscript shows the causal chain (letter → interception → capture) but does not explicitly record the promise's intended result and failure.
- What a fix would have to touch
  - Where: best done in s-003 (where the interception occurs) or s-004 (final scene). The least intrusive places:
    - Option A (s-003): add one explicit line when Lord Harrow reads the letter aloud or to himself that reveals its content or intention—e.g., a single sentence summing the note ("a plain petition to be taken away, a plea for a stolen life together")—so the ledger clearly links the sealed note to the intended escape.
    - Option B (s-004): add one line where the letter's existence and purpose are acknowledged in the courtyard (Elys referencing "the note" or Lord Harrow naming it when pronouncing the charge). That ties the sealed note to the motive and shows that the promise's aim was frustrated by interception.
  - Why this is minimal: it does not alter the chain of custody (we already have letter moving from Garr → intercepted → Lord Harrow) but makes explicit the letter's role as the escape plan that failed.
- Is the fix worth its risk?
  - Yes. Low risk and recommended. Clarifying the letter's content or purpose prevents the ledger from treating the writing of the letter as a dangling dramatic promise and shows that the lovers' scheme existed and failed by coercion/interception rather than by narrative neglect.

Overall recommended repair strategy (what I would actually do)
- Make two tiny, targeted additions only to s-004 (or one to s-003 and one to s-004) that explicitly register:
  1) Elys's recognition that the vow ("I will wait") has been broken by Garr's death, or Garr's last words directly addressing the promise (provenance: s-001 → s-004).
  2) A clear statement of what was in/for the sealed note (a line summarizing its purpose) so the ledger shows the letter attempted to bring about escape and was foiled (provenance: s-002 → s-003 → s-004).
- Keep each addition to a single sentence or two, placed where it dovetails with existing beats (Elys's last speech, Garr's last words, or Lord Harrow's pronouncement). This keeps changes minimal and avoids creating contradictions elsewhere.
- Logically this preserves the tragedy: the promises are not suddenly fulfilled; they are recorded as tried and failed. That conversion makes the absence readable as design and removes the "unpaid promise" flag without altering any established event chains.

Worth versus risk summary
- Both fixes are low-risk, high-value edits: they resolve ledger flags with minimal prose changes that do not contradict committed facts. They are worth doing.
- If you prefer to keep the manuscript text untouched, an alternative is to add a short continuity note (in continuity/ or with index-manager) that records the authorial intention: that these promises are deliberately denied as the thematic payoff. That also satisfies the ledger, but it separates the payoff from the prose rather than making it visible on the page. I still prefer the tiny prose clarifications in s-004 because they improve the reader experience and keep theme and ledger in alignment.

What I would do differently next time (already recorded)
- I attempted to store a working lesson as a remember entry: "promise-payoff-foreshadow" — procedural changes so future scenes that create tracked promises include an 'expected_payoff' field or an 'alternative_outcome' flag and, if ambiguous, a mandated foreshadowing beat soon afterwards. This is now in memory for the project and will be used in future planning.

If you want me to implement the recommended minimal fixes, say so and I will open a revision transaction (call which scenes you want changed: s-003 and/or s-004) and prepare a proposed state delta and exact lines to add. If you prefer only ledger/continuity notes (no prose edits), say that and I will prepare the continuity entries instead.
